passage.title: Cooling the city
passage.text:
On a summer afternoon, the center of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside around it. This “urban heat island” arises largely because pavement and roofs absorb sunlight and release the heat slowly, and because cities have few surfaces from which water can evaporate. Evaporation matters because turning water into vapor consumes heat: a wet field stays cooler than a dry parking lot in the same sun.

Planting trees is the most popular response. A tree cools its surroundings in two ways. Its canopy shades the ground and the walls of nearby buildings, keeping them from absorbing sunlight in the first place, and its leaves release water vapor, a process known as transpiration, which cools the surrounding air much as sweating cools the skin. Studies of neighborhoods with dense tree cover have found afternoon air temperatures noticeably lower than in comparable neighborhoods without it.

Yet the benefit is not the same everywhere. In humid cities, rain usually supplies all the water that trees need, but the moist air limits how much additional cooling transpiration can provide; most of a tree's value there comes from its shade. In arid cities the situation is reversed. Dry air allows transpiration to cool powerfully, but only if the trees are watered, and irrigation draws on water supplies that are often already strained. A tree that is not watered in such a climate may survive, but it closes the pores in its leaves to conserve water and delivers little more than shade.

None of this means that arid cities should stop planting trees. It does mean that the choice of species and the siting of each tree deserve as much attention as the number planted. In the driest cities, reflective “cool roofs,” which bounce sunlight back before it can be absorbed, can supply cooling that requires no water at all, leaving the available water for the trees that shade the streets where people walk.

diagnosis.why: Cool roofs appear only in the last paragraph, and only for the driest cities, as a complement to trees.
The author says the opposite: 'None of this means that arid cities should stop planting trees.'
The passage discusses water supplies, not costs, and does not compare costs.
Heat islands are explained only in the first paragraph, as background; the rest of the passage is about how well trees cool.

D: Heat islands are explained only in the first paragraph, as background; the rest of the passage is about how well trees cool.

passage.title: Pay what you want
passage.text:
When a restaurant or a band lets customers decide how much to pay, most observers expect the business to be exploited: why pay anything when nothing is required? Field experiments with “pay-what-you-want” pricing have repeatedly found that this expectation is too pessimistic. In several studies the great majority of customers paid something, and a sizable minority paid close to what the seller would normally have charged.

Researchers explain this behavior mainly by social motives rather than by generosity alone. Many customers appear to care about treating the seller fairly, and many care about how they will be seen by the seller or by other customers. These motives are strongest when the exchange is personal. In one experiment, customers who paid the owner of a café directly paid considerably more, on average, than customers who dropped their money into an anonymous box, even though the food and service were identical.

The same research suggests when the method is likely to succeed. It works best when the seller's cost of serving one more customer is low, because even modest payments then cover that cost; when customers can see the person they are paying; and when the product has a familiar reference price, which gives customers a sense of what a fair payment would be. Where these conditions are absent—where each unit is expensive to produce, where payment is anonymous, or where customers have no idea what the product is worth—sellers have fared poorly.

Pay-what-you-want pricing, in other words, is neither a charitable gesture nor a gimmick doomed to fail. It is a pricing strategy with a narrow but real field of application. Sellers who adopt it outside that field should not be surprised when their customers behave as the skeptics predicted.

diagnosis.why: The author calls the method's field of application 'narrow'.
The author criticizes only its use outside the right conditions, and defends the method within them.
The passage explains payments by social motives 'rather than by generosity alone'.

solution: A is correct: the passage answers the skeptics' expectation by showing why customers pay and when the method works. B: The author calls the method's field of application 'narrow'. C: The author criticizes only its use outside the right conditions, and defends the method within them. D: The passage explains payments by social motives 'rather than by generosity alone'. E: The café experiment is one piece of evidence, not the subject of the passage.

passage.title: The spread of standard time
passage.text:
Before the late nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time, setting their clocks by the sun so that noon fell when the sun stood highest. Because the sun's position changes as one moves east or west, clocks in two towns only a few dozen miles apart could differ by several minutes. For most of history the differences caused little trouble. Railroads changed that. A timetable listing dozens of stations, each with its own local time, confused passengers and, worse, endangered trains that shared a single track.

The standard account of what followed is simple: railroad companies divided the country into a few broad time zones, and the public, recognizing the convenience, soon adopted railroad time for everyday life. Recent historians have complicated this story. They point out that for years after the railroads adopted standard time, many towns continued to keep local time for civic purposes, and some kept both, displaying two sets of hands on public clocks. Opponents objected that time should follow the sun, not the needs of corporations, and a number of city councils voted to reject the new system before later accepting it.

What eventually spread standard time, these historians argue, was less the railroads' decision than a web of smaller changes. Telegraph companies began to transmit precise time signals from observatories, which jewelers and businesses used to set their clocks; schools and factories adopted fixed schedules; and legal disputes over deadlines pushed courts toward a single time that could be verified. Only decades later did national law make standard time official.

The episode illustrates a broader point about technological change: a new technology may create the need for a new social convention, but it does not by itself determine how, or how quickly, the convention is accepted.

Telegraph companies spread time signals; the passage says the railroads created the zones.
No economic losses are mentioned.
This is the background in the first paragraph, not the point the passage builds to.

solution: D is correct: the passage challenges the simple account (railroads decided, the public followed) with evidence of resistance and a web of other causes. A: The passage never compares the accuracy of the two systems. B: Telegraph companies spread time signals; the passage says the railroads created the zones. C: No economic losses are mentioned. E: This is the background in the first paragraph, not the point the passage builds to.

passage.title: Fire and closed cones
passage.text:
Many pine species release their seeds as soon as their cones ripen. Some, however, are “serotinous”: their cones are sealed shut with resin and can stay on the branch, closed, for years or even decades. The resin melts only at high temperatures, so the seeds are released in large numbers after a fire has passed through the forest. At first glance this strategy seems risky, since a tree that waits for a fire may die without ever releasing its seeds. In the right setting, however, it pays off. A fire clears away competing plants and the thick layer of needles on the forest floor, exposing bare soil and letting in sunlight, conditions in which pine seedlings grow well.

Whether serotiny is favored depends on how often fires occur. If fires are very frequent, young trees burn before they have produced cones, and neither strategy succeeds for long. If fires are rare, serotinous trees tend to die of age or disease with their seeds still locked away, while trees that release seeds every year have been replacing themselves all along. Serotiny is therefore most advantageous where fires return at intervals long enough for trees to mature but short enough that a stand is likely to burn within the lifetime of its trees.

A striking test of this reasoning comes from species in which serotiny varies among populations. Researchers studying such species have found that stands with a history of frequent crown fires contain a high proportion of serotinous trees, while stands of the same species where such fires have been rare contain few. The pattern suggests that serotiny is not a fixed trait of a species but one that shifts with local conditions, and it raises a concern: if changes in climate alter how often fires occur, forests adapted to one pattern of fire may be poorly suited to the next.
